examples.title: Measurement probabilities calculation
examples.question: For |ψ⟩ = (√3/2)|0⟩ + (1/2)|1⟩, find the measurement probabilities P(0) and P(1).

examples.title: Complex amplitude and phase
examples.question: For state (1/√2)|0⟩ + (i/√2)|1⟩, find the computational-basis probabilities P(0) and P(1).
examples.answer: P(0) = 50% and P(1) = 50%. The state differs from |+⟩ by relative phase (π/2) even though measurement in the computational basis is 50/50.

examples.title: Two Hadamards and Interference
examples.question: What happens when the Hadamard gate (H) is applied twice consecutively to |0⟩?
steps: The |1⟩ amplitudes cancel destructively (1/2 - 1/2 = 0) while the |0⟩ amplitudes add constructively (1/2 + 1/2 = 1).
examples.answer: The state returns deterministically to |0⟩ (100% probability of 0). This illustrates quantum interference.

examples.title: Creating an entangled Bell state
examples.question: What happens when starting from |00⟩, applying H to qubit 0, followed by CNOT with control q0 and target q1?
steps: Apply CNOT (q0 controls q1): When q0 is 0, q1 remains 0 (|00⟩). When q0 is 1, q1 flips to 1 (|11⟩).
Final state is the Bell state (|00⟩ + |11⟩)/√2.
examples.answer: Measurement gives |00⟩ with 50% probability and |11⟩ with 50% probability. The outcomes |01⟩ and |10⟩ never occur.

examples.title: Statevector Normalization Condition
examples.question: Why must |α|² + |β|² equal 1 for any valid one-qubit state α|0⟩ + β|1⟩?
steps: The squared magnitudes |α|² and |β|² represent the probabilities of mutually exclusive measurement outcomes 0 and 1.
The sum of probabilities for all possible outcomes in any physical measurement must equal 100% (1).
